title: FinTech, Lesson 4: Digital lending - approved in three seconds, and what that costs
subtitle: Credit risk cost in an app-based lending model, and why a high interest rate does not mean a high profit
whyItMatters: Lending is where fintech margins are fattest and also where companies die fastest. Knowing how to subtract risk cost from the interest earned is the difference between a product that makes money and a product that only looks like it does for the first two quarters.
openingQuestion: A loan charges 40% a year, cost of funds is 12%, operating cost is 6% and the loss rate is 25%. What margin is left?
openingOptions: Cannot be computed without knowing the average tenor of the loan
explanation: 40 − 12 − 6 − 25 = −3%. This product loses money, however high the headline rate sounds. That is the core misunderstanding about digital consumer lending: a high interest rate is not high profit, it is the price charged to cover a high loss rate. A product earning 40% with a 25% loss rate is decisively worse than one earning 18% with a 3% loss rate. Which is why the most important metric for a digital lending team is not disbursement volume but risk cost - and risk cost only reveals itself after a few months, exactly when the company has finished disbursing a large book.

realWorldExample.company: The wave of consumer lending apps, 2019-2022
realWorldExample.description: Dozens of apps entered the market with very high effective rates and approval in minutes. Most grew their loan books very fast in the first year - because bad debt had not yet had time to appear - and then vanished when the first cohort came due and the loss rate showed its true shape.

quiz.question: What is risk cost in a lending product?
options: The share of the loan book expected never to be recovered
The fee paid to the credit scoring data provider
The interest the company pays on the funds it borrows to lend on
The mandatory reserve the regulator requires it to deposit
quiz.explanation: Risk cost is the amount lost because customers do not repay. The interest paid on borrowed funds is cost of funds - an entirely separate line that has to be deducted on its own, and confusing the two is how a lending P&L ends up double-counting one deduction and missing another. Scoring fees are an operating cost, and regulatory reserves are a balance sheet requirement rather than a charge against margin.

quiz.question: Which product is better: 45% interest with a 28% loss rate, or 20% interest with a 4% loss rate?
options: The first one, because the interest rate is more than double
The second: the margin before other costs is 16% against 17%… but far more stable
Equal, because higher risk always comes with correspondingly higher return
The first, because the loss rate may fall as the scoring model learns more
quiz.explanation: The two margins are almost identical (17% and 16%), but the first product only needs the loss rate to worsen by a few points before it is lossmaking, while the second can absorb a much larger error. Risk and return moving together is a statement about efficient markets, not a guarantee that any given loan book is priced correctly. And betting on a scoring model improving is a plan, not a margin.

quiz.question: Why does the bad debt ratio of a fast-growing loan book look artificially low?
options: Because the accounting standards allow bad debt recognition to be deferred for two quarters
Because new loans always have better credit quality than older loans
Because the denominator swells faster than the old loans have time to go bad
Because new customers tend to repay on time in order to build a credit history
quiz.explanation: Bad debt takes time to surface while the loan book grows immediately. Dividing a slow numerator by a fast denominator always gives a flattering ratio - right up until growth slows. No accounting standard permits deferring recognition this way, and the new loans are not better quality; they are simply younger, which is a different thing entirely and the distinction the whole vintage method is built on.

quiz.question: What is the right way to read the credit quality of a fast-growing loan book?
options: Wait until year end and compute it on audited figures
Overdue balances divided by the total loan book
Compare the bad debt ratio against the industry average
Track each cohort separately by month of disbursement
quiz.explanation: Vintage analysis compares loans of the same age against each other, so growth cannot hide the trend. This is the standard tool of every credit risk team. Overdue over total book is precisely the ratio that growth distorts, an industry average has the same distortion baked in, and waiting for audited year-end figures gives you the same misleading ratio several months later.

quiz.question: When is approving a loan in three seconds acceptable?
options: When the loan is small enough that thorough underwriting costs more than the losses it prevents
When the company has enough capital to absorb any loss rate whatsoever
When the interest rate is high enough to cover every possible level of risk
Never, because an automated decision is always worse than underwriting carried out by a human being
quiz.explanation: This is a cost trade-off. On a loan of a few million dong, a verification phone call costs more than the money it saves; on a loan of a few hundred million it is the other way round entirely. Capital to absorb losses is a buffer, not a reason to stop underwriting, and no rate covers every possible risk level - that is the belief the opening calculation of this lesson disproves.

practicePrompt.question: A loan book is growing 12% a month, the bad debt ratio on total balances is 2.1% and it has fallen steadily for six months. What is the correct conclusion?
options: No conclusion yet, because the denominator is moving faster than the numerator
Credit quality is clearly improving with each passing month
Bad debt of 2.1% is a safe level for digital consumer lending
The company needs to grow even faster in order to keep diluting the bad debt ratio
practicePrompt.explanation: A loan takes several months to go bad, so the numerator reflects older disbursement cohorts while the denominator has already absorbed every new cohort, all still too young to fail. The faster the book grows, the better the ratio looks - and it looks best right before the new cohorts come of age. The correct reading is to split by cohort: take the customers who borrowed in January, see what percentage has failed after six months, then compare against February and March. The 'grow faster to dilute it' option describes the trap accurately, it just mistakes it for a solution.

keyTakeaways: A high interest rate is the price of high risk, not a sign of high profit.
Real margin = interest earned − cost of funds − operating cost − risk cost. Missing the last term is missing the decisive one.
A fast-growing book always has a flattering bad debt ratio, because the denominator moves faster than the numerator.
Read by disbursement cohort, not by total book.

summary.keyIdea: A high interest rate is the price of high risk, not a sign of high profit
summary.formula: Real margin = interest earned − cost of funds − operating cost − risk cost
summary.commonMistake: Reading the bad debt ratio on a fast-growing total book - the denominator moves faster than the numerator, so the figure always flatters.
summary.action: Ask for the data by monthly disbursement cohort rather than by total book, then compare cohorts of the same age.

application.title: Read a loan book by disbursement cohort
application.message: Take the overdue rate of the loans disbursed in January when they were six months old, then compare it against the rate of the June cohort also at six months old. That is the only comparison that means anything.
application.secondary: If the later cohort is worse than the earlier one at the same age, underwriting quality is deteriorating even though the total book still looks fine.

sections.text: Lending carries the fattest margin in fintech, and it is also the segment that makes companies disappear fastest. Both of those come from the same number: the money that never comes back.

sections.title: The contribution margin of a lending product
sections.equation: Margin = interest and fees − cost of funds − operating cost − risk cost

variables.name: the price of money
variables.description: the interest the company pays on the funding it borrows in order to lend on

variables.name: the losses
variables.description: the share of the loan book expected not to be recovered

example.title: A small consumer loan
example.explanation: The rate sounds very high and the product still loses money. The decisive number is the 25%, not the 40%.

sections.text: Why bad debt always shows up late

A loan only goes bad after several repayment cycles. Meanwhile the loan book grows the moment money is disbursed. Dividing a numerator that arrives late by a denominator that arrives immediately will always produce a flattering ratio, and that ratio only deteriorates once growth slows - which is to say, exactly when the company has finished disbursing a very large cohort.

left.label: Reading the total book
left.text: Overdue balances / total loan book. Fast growth dilutes this figure and hides the real trend.

right.label: Reading by cohort
right.text: Compare loans of the same age: the March cohort at 6 months, the April cohort at 6 months. Growth hides nothing.

sections.label: The question to ask in every lending product meeting
sections.text: Not 'how much did we disburse this month' but 'is the cohort from six months ago performing worse or better than the cohort from twelve months ago'. The first question measures speed, the second measures quality - and only the second gives you warning.

lines: A good lending product is not the one with the highest rate, it is the one with the widest gap between interest earned and risk cost.
And that gap can only be measured once the first loans are old enough.
